# Brunn–Minkowski for simplex-source body arrays, with exact nonrigidity

Fix affinely independent bases \(p_1,\ldots,p_N\in\mathbb R^n\), positive coefficients \(\lambda_i\) of sum one, and

\[
j=\sum_i\lambda_i p_i.
\]

Let \(\mathcal A=(A_i)_{i=1}^N\) be an array of full-dimensional compact convex bodies in \(\mathbb R^d\), \(d\ge1\). Its source measure is the sum of the **unnormalized** \(d\)-volume laws on \(\{p_i\}\times A_i\). Define

\[
D_{\mathcal A}=\sum_i\lambda_i A_i,\qquad
p_{\mathcal A}(y)=\inf_{H\ni(j,y)}\mu_{\mathcal A}(H)
\quad (y\in D_{\mathcal A}),
\]

where all ambient closed halfspaces are allowed. For a second array \(\mathcal B=(B_i)\) and \(0\le t\le1\), put

\[
K_i=(1-t)A_i+tB_i,\qquad \mathcal K=(K_i).
\]

Then the following joint body-and-center inequality holds:

\[
p_{\mathcal K}((1-t)y+tz)^{1/d}
\ \ge\
(1-t)p_{\mathcal A}(y)^{1/d}
+t p_{\mathcal B}(z)^{1/d}
\tag{1}
\]

for every \(y\in D_{\mathcal A}\), \(z\in D_{\mathcal B}\). In particular the attained fixed-base maximal depth

\[
\mathcal M(\mathcal A)=\max_{y\in D_{\mathcal A}}p_{\mathcal A}(y)
\]

satisfies

\[
\mathcal M((1-t)\mathcal A+t\mathcal B)^{1/d}
\ge(1-t)\mathcal M(\mathcal A)^{1/d}
+t\mathcal M(\mathcal B)^{1/d}.
\tag{2}
\]

These are source-measure statements at the fixed barycentric base. They do not remove additional integer fibers of a convex hull. Affine independence is essential to the threshold argument; no affinely dependent array theorem is asserted.

An archive search found the earlier ordinary one-body theorem and a counterexample for normalized depth on dependent compatible arrays. Neither is the assertion here. The source quantile ingredients were proved in candidate 0fcbc670d417c3ed, Sections 1–6, and are recalled with the needed boundary qualifications below.

## 1. One-body quantiles under Minkowski interpolation

For a full-dimensional body \(A\), a unit vector \(u\), and \(0\le r\le |A|^{1/d}\), let \(q_{A,u}(r)\) be the threshold of its upper cap of volume \(r^d\). At the endpoints it is the maximum support value for \(r=0\) and the minimum support value for \(r=|A|^{1/d}\). These quantiles are continuous and strictly decreasing.

If \(K=(1-t)A+tB\), cap Brunn–Minkowski implies

\[
q_{K,u}((1-t)r+ts)
\ge(1-t)q_{A,u}(r)+tq_{B,u}(s).
\tag{3}
\]

Indeed the Minkowski combination of the two quantile cap bodies lies in the \(K\)-cap at the threshold on the right and has volume root at least \((1-t)r+ts\). Since cap volume decreases with threshold, its quantile threshold cannot be smaller. A zero-volume quantile cap is a **nonempty supporting face**, so its use in this inclusion is valid. Full-volume endpoint caps are the whole bodies. Ordinary volume Brunn–Minkowski also puts the argument on the left in its allowed domain. Cases \(t=0,1\) are immediate.

## 2. Fixed allocations and the plateau

For each array write

\[
R_{\mathcal A}^*=\min_i|A_i|^{1/d},\qquad
\Omega_N=\{\alpha_i\ge0:\ \sum_i\alpha_i^d=1\},
\]

and, for \(0\le R\le R_{\mathcal A}^*\), set

\[
Q_{\mathcal A,u}(R)
=\min_{\alpha\in\Omega_N}
\sum_i\lambda_i q_{A_i,u}(R\alpha_i).
\tag{4}
\]

The allocation set is compact and independent of \(R\) and of the bodies. All arguments stay in their quantile domains.

For fixed \(u\), the endpoint thresholds of an ambient cap through \((j,y)\) are free subject to exactly

\[
\sum_i\lambda_i t_i=u\cdot y.
\tag{5}
\]

Affine independence proves sufficiency: interpolate the values \(u\cdot y-t_i\) on the bases by an affine function. Their barycentric average is zero, so this function is a linear form in \(p_i-j\). Necessity follows by averaging the same cap equation.

Define the optimized directional source cost

\[
C_{\mathcal A,u}(s)
=\inf_{\sum_i\lambda_i t_i=s}
\sum_i |A_i\cap\{u\cdot x\ge t_i\}|.
\]

For \(0<R<R_{\mathcal A}^*\), the exact strict equivalence is

\[
C_{\mathcal A,u}(s)<R^d
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
s>Q_{\mathcal A,u}(R).
\tag{6}
\]

It follows by lowering or raising quantile thresholds at a fixed allocation, as proved in the cited source. Its strict range ensures that no allocated volume is a full endpoint mass; zero allocated volumes are permitted. The profile equals the smallest full source volume on the left plateau \(s\le Q_{\mathcal A,u}(R_{\mathcal A}^*)\), is the inverse profile in the middle, and vanishes at and beyond

\[
Q_{\mathcal A,u}(0)=h_{D_{\mathcal A}}(u).
\]

For \(N\ge2\), the fixed-direction upper plateau bound follows by setting all other thresholds sufficiently high and the chosen smallest-source threshold sufficiently low in (5). For \(N=1\), the sole threshold is fixed; its ordinary cap volume is already at most the full body volume. The one-body inverse and plateau statements remain valid.

Consequently, if \(y\in D_{\mathcal A}\) and \(R=p_{\mathcal A}(y)^{1/d}\), then

\[
0\le R\le R_{\mathcal A}^*,\qquad
u\cdot y\le Q_{\mathcal A,u}(R)\quad\text{for every unit }u.
\tag{7}
\]

For \(0<R<R_{\mathcal A}^*\), use (6). For \(R=R_{\mathcal A}^*\), take the limit from below and use quantile continuity. For \(R=0\), use \(y\in D_{\mathcal A}\) and the support identity. Thus (7) does not apply a strict-mass formula incorrectly at either endpoint.

## 3. The common-allocation proof

Put

\[
R_A=p_{\mathcal A}(y)^{1/d},\qquad
R_B=p_{\mathcal B}(z)^{1/d},\qquad
R=(1-t)R_A+tR_B.
\]

For every \(i\), ordinary volume Brunn–Minkowski gives

\[
R\le(1-t)|A_i|^{1/d}+t|B_i|^{1/d}
\le |K_i|^{1/d}.
\tag{8}
\]

Thus \(R\le R_{\mathcal K}^*\). For **every same allocation** \(\alpha\in\Omega_N\), apply (3) with arguments \(R_A\alpha_i,R_B\alpha_i\), then sum with the fixed coefficients \(\lambda_i\). Taking minima yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_{\mathcal K,u}(R)
&\ge\min_{\alpha\in\Omega_N}
\left[(1-t)\sum_i\lambda_i q_{A_i,u}(R_A\alpha_i)
+t\sum_i\lambda_i q_{B_i,u}(R_B\alpha_i)\right]\\
&\ge(1-t)Q_{\mathcal A,u}(R_A)
+tQ_{\mathcal B,u}(R_B)\\
&\ge u\cdot((1-t)y+tz).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

The minima for the two arrays are not required to have a common optimizer; the second inequality is simply that every combined value is at least the corresponding sum of separate minima.

The target point belongs to

\[
D_{\mathcal K}=(1-t)D_{\mathcal A}+tD_{\mathcal B}.
\]

Equations (6)–(9), including the plateau and zero-depth cases, show that every nonvertical containing cap has mass at least \(R^d\). A purely base-normal cap through \(j\) contains at least one entire source because \(j\) is a positive barycentric combination of its bases. Its mass is at least \(\min_i|K_i|\ge R^d\). A containing cap can be translated to pass through the candidate while only decreasing its mass. This proves (1) for all closed caps.

## 4. Attainment, scaling, and strict common thickening

For a fixed finite array, its depth at the fixed base \(j\) is a Lipschitz function of the continuous center. Normalize the nonzero continuous normal to one. Moving the center by \(h\) shifts every source threshold by the same scalar of magnitude at most \(\lVert h\rVert\), independent of the size of the base tilt. A containing ball for each body gives a uniform slab-volume upper bound; the sum of these finitely many bounds is a common Lipschitz constant. Purely base-normal cap masses are constant under this movement. Taking the infimum preserves the bound.

The set \(D_{\mathcal A}\) is compact. Its interior points represented by interior points of every source have positive depth, because a containing halfspace contains at least one of those source points and each has positive ordinary own depth. Thus \(\mathcal M(\mathcal A)\) is positive and attained. Applying (1) to chosen maximizers proves (2).

Common continuous scaling multiplies source depth by the \(d\)-th power of the scale. Therefore (1)–(2) also give the homogeneous positive-coefficient versions for arrays \(s\mathcal A+t\mathcal B\), with the same bases and barycentric coefficients.

Monotonicity under componentwise inclusion is immediate at any retained center. More quantitatively, if a second array satisfies

\[
L_i\supseteq A_i+\varepsilon B_d\quad\text{for every }i
\]

with \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(B_d\) the unit Euclidean ball, then

\[
\mathcal M(\mathcal L)^{1/d}
\ge\mathcal M(\mathcal A)^{1/d}
+\varepsilon\mathcal M((B_d)_i)^{1/d}
\ge\mathcal M(\mathcal A)^{1/d}
+\varepsilon(|B_d|/2)^{1/d}.
\tag{10}
\]

For the final inequality evaluate the equal-ball array at continuous center zero: every cap through the positive barycentric combination of the ball centers contains at least one center, and that source contributes at least half a ball. In particular, simultaneous strict interior containment \(A_i\subset\operatorname{int}L_i\) for every component implies strict increase, because a finite array admits a common positive \(\varepsilon\).

## 5. Exact equality and strict-inclusion nonrigidity

Array equality does **not** force homothety of the entire source bodies. It also does not imply strict monotonicity when only one component is enlarged.

Here is an exact all-dimensional plateau. Use two source bases \(0,1\), target \(j=1/2\), and let \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) be full-dimensional and centrally symmetric about zero. If

\[
L\supseteq K,
\]

then

\[
\mathcal M((K,L))=|K|,
\qquad p_{(K,L)}(0)=|K|.
\tag{11}
\]

The vertical cap containing the first source alone bounds depth at every point of the target plane by \(|K|\). For the lower bound at zero, the two thresholds of any nonvertical cap are \(h,-h\). Since \(L\supseteq K\), their combined mass is at least

\[
|K\cap\{u\cdot x\ge h\}|
+|K\cap\{u\cdot x\ge-h\}|=|K|.
\]

Reflection in the origin identifies the second cap with the complementary lower cap at \(h\); the separating hyperplane has zero \(d\)-volume. This includes empty, full, and supporting thresholds. Purely base-normal caps also capture at least \(|K|\). This proves (11) without any smoothness or limit.

For example, put

\[
K=[-1,1]^d,\quad L=[-3,3]^d,\quad
L'=[-4,4]\times[-3,3]^{d-1}.
\]

Every interpolation between the arrays \((K,L)\) and \((K,L')\) has maximal source depth \(|K|=2^d\), so (2) is equality throughout. The second source grows by proper inclusion, and for \(d\ge2\) its two shapes are not positively homothetic. Even in dimension one there is no common homothety ratio for the whole arrays: the unchanged first source forces ratio one while the other length changes.

This does not conflict with the ordinary one-body equality theorem or strict proper-inclusion theorem, recovered when \(N=1\). The source-array plateau comes from an entire-source cap budget and must be retained in any stronger equality analysis.

## 6. An exact interval calibration

For independent interval sources with centers \(c_i\), lengths \(l_i>0\), and fixed \(\lambda_i>0\), set

\[
\bar c=\sum_i\lambda_i c_i,\quad
H=\tfrac12\sum_i\lambda_i l_i,\quad
\Lambda=\max_i\lambda_i,\quad m=\min_i l_i.
\]

The quantiles in (4) are affine, giving the exact formulas

\[
p_{\mathcal A}(y)
=\min\{m,(H-|y-\bar c|)/\Lambda\}
\quad (|y-\bar c|\le H),
\qquad
\mathcal M(\mathcal A)=\min\{m,H/\Lambda\}.
\tag{12}
\]

They include \(N=1\), and directly exhibit both the body-array concavity and the full-source plateau. The standard-library verifier ../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_simplex_source_array_depth_bm.py checks (12) against finite exact threshold minimization for two and three independent sources and then checks joint array/center interpolation. These finite tests are diagnostics; Sections 1–5 give the general proof and the all-dimensional nonrigidity certificate.

## 7. Dependent arrays can fail after optimizing every center

Affine independence cannot be dropped even from the maximal-depth conclusion (2). Use three actual integer bases \(-1,0,1\), fixed endpoint intervals

\[
K_-=K_+=[-1/2,1/2],
\]

and the middle interval

\[
B_s=[s-5,s+5],\qquad 0\le s\le2.
\]

All these arrays are actual compatible convex families: the middle interval contains the endpoint Minkowski average. They have three positive fibers, and their total mixed mass is the constant 12.

The independently proved candidate 5048c7e97ca98aef, with \(a=b=1\) and \(U=10\), gives the exact optimized depth at the fixed middle base

\[
F_s=
\begin{cases}
6-s/2,&0\le s\le1,\\
11/2,&1\le s\le2.
\end{cases}
\tag{13}
\]

The exposed endpoint maxima are \(1/2\), so \(F_s\) is also the maximum over the entire original mixed-integer set. Componentwise Minkowski averaging of the arrays at \(s=0\) and \(s=2\) gives the array at \(s=1\), but

\[
F_1=11/2<\tfrac12(6+11/2)=23/4.
\]

In fact every positive power fails concavity on this segment: \(F_1=F_2<F_0\), hence

\[
F_1^p<\tfrac12(F_0^p+F_2^p)\qquad(p>0).
\]

Equivalently the positive-value slope jumps from \(-1/2\) to zero at \(s=1\). This is a full optimized-depth obstruction in dimension \(d=1\), stronger than merely finding nonconcavity at prescribed continuous points. No higher-dimensional product extension is asserted.

## 8. Symmetric dependent arrays fail in every higher dimension

There is a different, entirely concentric obstruction in every \(d\ge2\). Let \(K=-K\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional compact convex body, with volume \(V>0\). For \(R\ge1\), use the actual three integer fibers

\[
K_{-1}=K,\qquad K_0=RK,\qquad K_1=K.
\tag{14}
\]

Their convex hull is compact and full-dimensional. The forced endpoint average is \(K\subseteq RK\), so its three integer fibers are exactly (14); there are no other integer bases. Thus its original mixed measure has total

\[
T_R=V(2+R^d).
\]

The entire source is centrally symmetric about the actual point \((0,0)\). For any closed through-origin halfspace, reflection exchanges it with its opposite and preserves the source measure. Its mass is therefore \((T_R+\mu(\partial H))/2\ge T_R/2\). This explicitly retains possible positive boundary mass on a vertical cap. Any merely containing cap includes its parallel through-origin cap.

Conversely, at **any** candidate, choose any nonzero continuous normal and the two complementary closed through-candidate caps. Their common boundary cuts every full-dimensional fiber in a set of zero \(d\)-volume. Their masses sum to \(T_R\), so one has mass at most \(T_R/2\). Consequently both the maximum restricted to the middle fiber and the global mixed maximum are exactly

\[
\mathcal M_R=T_R/2=V(R^d/2+1).
\tag{15}
\]

This is an absolute maximum, not a lower bound from symmetry alone.

Componentwise Minkowski interpolation of the arrays at \(R_0,R_1\) replaces \(R\) by \((1-t)R_0+tR_1\), with the endpoints unchanged. But the normalized root of (15) is strictly convex:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi(R)&=(R^d/2+1)^{1/d},\\
\phi''(R)&=\frac{d-1}{2}\,
R^{d-2}(R^d/2+1)^{1/d-2}>0
\qquad(d\ge2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}
\]

Thus the strict opposite of array root-BM holds for every pair of distinct radii and every interior interpolation parameter. All bodies in this example are concentric homothetic, and the optimizing point can be kept at the same actual middle point throughout.

For a completely explicit planar witness take a unit-area symmetric square and \(R=1,2,3\). The three exact maxima are \(3/2,3,11/2\). The proposed root-concavity inequality would imply

\[
\sqrt3\ge\frac{\sqrt{3/2}+\sqrt{11/2}}2,
\]

equivalently \(5\ge\sqrt{33}\), contradicted by \(25<33\).

The same family also gives a local failure for **every positive power**, rather than only \(1/d\). For \(q>0\), putting \(S=R^d/2+1\) gives

\[
\frac{d^2}{dR^2}S^q
=\frac{qd}{2}\,R^{d-2}S^{q-2}
\left[(d-1)+\frac{dq-1}{2}R^d\right].
\tag{17}
\]

For \(1\le R\le1+1/(2d)\), the finite binomial estimate

\[
R^d\le(1+1/(2d))^d
\le\sum_{k=0}^d2^{-k}<2
\]

makes the bracket strictly positive: it equals
\((d-1)-R^d/2+dqR^d/2\), whose first two terms already have positive sum when \(d\ge2\). Hence the three fixed radii

\[
1,\qquad 1+\frac1{4d},\qquad 1+\frac1{2d}
\]

give a strict midpoint violation simultaneously for every positive power \(q\). This is a direct same-dimensional construction, not an assumed product transfer of the translated-interval example.

All normalized original maximum depths in (14) are exactly \(1/2\). The counterexamples concern concavity of the **unnormalized** optimized source functional under dependent-array interpolation; they are not OC failures.

## 9. Ordinary depth in the actual Minkowski section

Retain the affinely independent source assumptions and positive barycentric weights of Sections 1–4. Write
\[
D=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_iK_i,\qquad
c_\lambda=
\begin{cases}
\left(\sum_i\lambda_i^{d/(d-1)}\right)^{d-1},&d>1,\\
\max_i\lambda_i,&d=1.
\end{cases}
\]
Let \(f_D(y)\) be the unnormalized ordinary halfspace depth of \(y\) in the uniform body \(D\). Then, at the same continuous point \(y\in D\),
\[
f_D(y)\ \ge\ c_\lambda\,p_{\mathcal K}(y).
\tag{18}
\]

To prove this, the zero-depth case is immediate. Otherwise put
\(R=p_{\mathcal K}(y)^{1/d}>0\). The full-source bound gives
\(R\le\min_i|K_i|^{1/d}\). Fix any nonzero continuous normal \(u\). The established threshold characterization, including the full-source plateau by continuity from below, gives
\[
\sum_i\lambda_iq_{i,u}(R\alpha_i)
\ge Q_{\mathcal K,u}(R)\ge u\cdot y
\]
for every \(\alpha_i\ge0\) with \(\sum_i\alpha_i^d=1\).
For each \(i\), take the closed cap
\(E_i=K_i\cap\{u\cdot x\ge q_{i,u}(R\alpha_i)\}\).
It has volume \((R\alpha_i)^d\). If \(\alpha_i=0\), it is a nonempty supporting face; if \(R\alpha_i=|K_i|^{1/d}\), it is the whole body. Consequently
\[
\sum_i\lambda_iE_i
\subseteq D\cap\{u\cdot x\ge u\cdot y\}.
\]
Brunn–Minkowski for these nonempty compact convex sets gives
\[
\bigl|D\cap\{u\cdot x\ge u\cdot y\}\bigr|^{1/d}
\ge R\sum_i\lambda_i\alpha_i.
\]
Maximizing the right side over the fixed allocation set is precisely Hölder duality: its maximum is
\(\|\lambda\|_{d/(d-1)}\) for \(d>1\), and \(\max_i\lambda_i\) for \(d=1\). Raising to the \(d\)-th power and taking the infimum over \(u\) proves (18). A containing closed cap contains its parallel through-point cap, so this covers the ordinary depth convention completely.

For two midpoint sources, \(c_\lambda=1/2\) in every dimension, hence
\[
p_{\mathcal K}(y)\le2f_{(K_1+K_2)/2}(y).
\tag{19}
\]
More generally equal weights on \(N\) sources give \(c_\lambda=1/N\). The singleton case is the identity \(p_K=f_K\). This is a same-point comparison and an upper bound on the paired-source depth; it supplies no additional mixed-integer lower bound and requires no assertion about equality.
